issues.issue: Exculpation turns on acts done "in good faith" and "in a manner reasonably believed to be within the scope of authority," with the carve-out for "gross negligence or willful misconduct" left undefined. Where that line falls is classically contestable.

The exculpation runs in favour of every Covered Person, including a Member, while Section 7.7 imposes corporate-style duties of loyalty and care on Directors and Officers; the interaction of the two standards is not spelled out.

The provision as it appears is a fragment beginning mid-sentence ("professional or expert competence and who has been selected with reasonable care"), with the operative reliance language missing. There is no ascertainable rule to apply.

The section says the Agreement's provisions "replace" other duties "to the extent that they restrict" them, without identifying which provisions do the restricting. Whether common-law fiduciary duties survive is left to argument.

This wholesale replacement of fiduciary duties cannot be squared with Section 7.7, which affirmatively imposes on each Director and Officer the duties of loyalty and care of a Maine business corporation.

Indemnification is promised to every Covered Person, a class far wider than "the Members and Managers," whereas Section 17.11 provides that nothing confers rights under the Agreement on any Person except Members and Managers.

Advancement is mandatory here on a bare undertaking, while Section 6.8(xiv) forbids the incurrence of any material liability or obligation without unanimous Board approval. Whether advancement to a member-litigant needs Board approval is unresolved.
The sentence breaks off at "against any liability that may be asserted," so the scope of the insurance permitted is never completed. The clause cannot be applied as written.

The first sentence is missing words — "and the Company the income or profits derived therefrom" — so it never says what the Company's rights in that income are. The freedom-to-compete grant is unintelligible at its centre.

"DMSA does agree that it intends to use diligent efforts to direct appropriate business to the Company" is a statement of intention rather than a promise, and "appropriate business" and "diligent efforts" are unmeasured. Whether DMSA undertook any enforceable obligation is genuinely arguable.

"LSB shall not provide such services" has no antecedent for "such services," and the covenant is bounded only by "to the extent it relates to the business," a phrase with no definition, duration or geographic limit. What LSB may lawfully do outside the Company turns entirely on construing this sentence.

The clause imposes exclusivity on LSB alone within a section that expressly frees DMSA to compete and relieves it of fiduciary duty, and "the business" must be filled in from Section 3.1's open-ended purpose clause. The asymmetry and the missing referent leave the covenant unreconcilable on its own terms.
DMSA is a Member, not a Director, yet the clause relieves it of "its fiduciary duties as a Director"; whether the relief reaches DMSA's Member duties or its elected Directors' duties is unclear.

Section 7.7 imposes on each Director the fiduciary duties of loyalty and care of a Maine business corporation, and this clause purports to remove them for DMSA; the two provisions point in opposite directions.

Disclosure is barred without "the prior written consent of the LLC," but "LLC" is not a defined term (the entity is "the Company") and the first sentence obliges the parties to keep confidential "all efforts and actions undertaken by them," a scope untethered to the defined Proprietary Information. The obligation's reach is uncertain.

The blanket confidentiality obligation binds DMSA equally, yet Section 12.7 authorises DMSA to pursue competing ventures and to recommend opportunities to others; the two are difficult to operate together.

"Proprietary Information" is defined by a closed list ending in "advertiser provided information, documents and data," with no catch-all and no carve-out for publicly available or independently obtained material. Whether, for example, subscriber contacts already public fall inside is arguable.

Admission requires the approval of all Members here, while Section 16.3 makes a transferee's mere written undertaking to become a party sufficient for a valid transfer and Section 16.8 lets the Board waive transfer restrictions unilaterally. The routes to membership are inconsistent.

The prohibition is circular — no assignment "without complying with the terms of this Agreement" — and does not identify which terms govern assignment. The operative restriction has to be assembled from elsewhere.

A pledge requires the prior written consent of all Members here, while Section 16.8 allows the Board, "[n]otwithstanding anything to the contrary," to waive any transfer restriction in the Agreement. The two cannot both control a pledge.

Clause (ii) makes the "resignation" of a Member a dissolution event, but Section 5.4 provides that a Member may not resign before dissolution and winding up; the trigger cannot occur under the Agreement's own terms.

The direction that "[t]he Members shall continue to distribute Interest Profits and Losses" uses a term found nowhere in Article I and puts the distribution in the Members' hands although the Board conducts the winding up. The sentence is garbled.

Liquidating proceeds go out on Capital Account balances, while Sections 8.1 and 9.1 allocate and distribute on Percentage Interests; with Schedule A recording contributions of $50,000 against $00,001 for a 51/49 split, the two measures produce sharply different outcomes.

Transfers are recorded on Schedule A, which under Section 2.1(iii) the Secretary may update unilaterally without that being an amendment; ownership of record could thus shift without the Member consents Article XVI requires.

"Transfer" is defined to reach involuntary transfers and transfers "by division of marital property or otherwise," while excepting only a revocable proxy; the reach of the "or otherwise" residue against the enumerated specifics is uncertain.

The sanction is that the Interests "will be deemed not to be voted," which cannot be reconciled with Section 5.5(vii)-(viii), where quorum and Majority Vote are computed from the Member Votes fixed by Schedule A. Whether the suspended votes drop out of the denominator is unaddressed.

A transferee becomes a valid holder simply by delivering a written undertaking, whereas Section 13.1 admits new members only "[b]y approval of all of the Members." The Agreement does not say whether such a transferee is a Member.
The section breaks off mid-sentence ("the parties agree that the Company and the other Members shall") and states no waiver rule at all. There is nothing operative to apply.
It applies to transfers "pursuant to Sections 16.9, 16.10, and 16.11 of this Agreement," but Article XVI ends at Section 16.8, so the triggering provisions do not exist in the instrument.

The Board or President may waive the securities-opinion requirement "for good cause," and the opinion must be "in form and substance Satisfactory" to them, with no standard for either judgment. Both phrases are open to competing readings.

The acceptance sentence runs straight into the allocation sentence with no acceptance deadline stated, yet the clause later refers to acceptance not occurring "within the periods set forth above." The missing period makes the mechanism unworkable as written.
The notice must state "the number of LLC Votes to be transferred," a term used nowhere else; the defined term in Article I is "Member Votes."

"Notwithstanding anything to the contrary," the Board may waive any transfer restriction, which nullifies the all-Member consents required by Section 14.3 for pledges and by Section 13.1 for admissions, and the right of first refusal in Section 16.6. A minority Member's protections could be removed by the majority-elected Board.

Notices to the Company go to the address "specified in Section 2.5," which the Board may change at any time, and no method is given for notifying Members of the change. The notice regime is incomplete but workable.

The clause is written backwards: it says failure to insist on performance "shall not prevent a subsequent act ... from having the effect of an original violation," which reads as preserving violations rather than as an anti-waiver rule, and "original violation" is undefined. The sentence's operation is doubtful.

The merger clause supersedes prior agreements only "pertaining to the subject matter hereof," a boundary that decides whether side understandings about LSB's employment or DMSA's services survive. That boundary is regularly fought over.

Maine law is chosen for an entity whose principal place of business is in Massachusetts and whose members are a Massachusetts resident and a New Jersey corporation, which invites argument about the reach of the clause over non-contract claims. The clause itself is clear, however.

Amendments require the affirmative vote and signature of all Members, yet Section 2.1(iii) permits the Secretary to revise Schedule A — which fixes Percentage Interests and Member Votes — and declares that revision not to be an amendment. The unanimity protection can be bypassed.

Rights are confined to "the Members and Managers," which excludes the wider class of Covered Persons expressly given indemnification and expense advancement by Sections 12.4 and 12.5. The two provisions cannot both be given full effect.
